Volume 18 · Chapter 05

Negotiation, conflict and stakeholder decisions

Professional Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v18-c04

By the endNegotiate institutional decisions using incentives, alternatives and principled process.

Volume 18 · Chapter 5

Negotiation, conflict and stakeholder decisions

Capability. Prepare and defend an institutional agreement using credible alternatives, consistent payoff accounts, explicit distribution choices and an implementable process. Recognize when changing the split cannot repair the problem. Prerequisite: Hiring, evaluation and talent development, especially recorded evidence, authority and correction; recall participation constraints and feasible transfers. Every institution, valuation, offer, conversation and agreement below is original and fictional. These are decision exercises, not executed negotiations or legal contract advice.

1. Prepare the alternative before arguing about the offer

A position is a requested term: “We need a fee of 70.” An interest is a reason behind it: funding delivery, preserving a standard, using staff effectively or avoiding an unreliable timetable. Distinguishing them creates questions rather than requiring surrender. A different delivery method might meet both parties' interests at lower cost; a cheaper promise that cannot meet the standard does not.

A BATNA, the best alternative to a negotiated agreement, is the best feasible action available if this negotiation fails. The Program on Negotiation's official BATNA introduction uses the outside alternative as the benchmark for evaluating an offer. Here we require a specific action, its date, costs, constraints and evidence of availability. An aspiration, an expired offer or an option requiring the other party's ungranted consent is not a ready fallback. Another negotiated deal can be an alternative to this one if it is actually available.

The reservation condition says what an agreement must deliver to be at least as good as the fallback. It is not necessarily the opening demand. Compare like with like: net benefit with net benefit, the same horizon and risk assumptions. If another contract produces revenue 30 but costs 20 to deliver, its net payoff is 10, not 30. If taking the new agreement prevents that contract, require new net payoff at least 10; do not also deduct the foregone 10 from new profit and then require that reduced amount to exceed 10. That would count the same opportunity twice.

Separate economic acceptability from authority and implementation. A negotiator may be able to explain why a payment is attractive but lack authority or cash to make it. Identify who can approve the scope, money and unresolved risks. Preserve confidential information appropriately; learning the other party's interests does not justify deception, invented threats or unauthorized disclosure. A strong fallback can support a credible refusal, but bargaining power does not prove that a proposed distribution is ethically justified.

2. Feasibility, gains and a transparent sharing rule

Consider a payer U and a provider L. A delivery mode creates gross benefit V for U, costs c for L and transfers t from U to L. Payoffs in common currency units are U=V−t and L=t−c. The transfer changes their distribution but cancels from total V−c. Suppose their mutually compatible outside payoffs are dU and dL, both nonnegative here, and U can pay at most B upfront. With nonnegative transfers and no borrowing, both participate exactly when

c+dL≤t≤min{V−dU,B}.

If the lower endpoint exceeds the upper, no acceptable funded agreement exists in this menu. If they coincide, only one transfer works, and at least one condition binds; no strict improvement for both is implied. Before the cash limit, joint gains over disagreement are S=V−c−dU−dL. Positive S is necessary for both to gain strictly, but it is not sufficient when the cash limit prevents compensation. Benefits measured by willingness to pay are not the cash available to pay.

A distribution rule must be stated rather than smuggled into “efficient.” Let x=V−t−dU be U's gain and S−x=t−c−dL be L's. One stipulated rule maximizes xα(S−x)1−α with 0<α<1. The weight α is an explicit bargaining convention, not an observed psychological trait or moral entitlement. At α=1/2 this is equivalent to maximizing the product of the two gains, the Nash bargaining objective described in Mihai Manea's MIT cooperative-games notes. We derive our restricted model directly; we do not claim to derive an actual negotiation process or the full axiomatic theorem.

Global solution. For S>0 and positive gains, maximize α log x+(1−α)log(S−x). Its derivative is α/x−(1−α)/(S−x), zero only at x=αS; its second derivative is strictly negative. Thus the unique unconstrained division is (αS,(1−α)S), or t*=c+dL+(1−α)S. On any nonempty transfer interval, the product rises toward that point and falls after it, so clip t* to the interval's endpoints if necessary. A feasible endpoint with zero gain is handled by the original product, not by taking log zero. If S=0 and participation is feasible, the interval is a singleton and both gains are zero; if S<0, participation is impossible. The weight endpoints α=0 or 1 are outside this positive-weight rule.

Compare delivery modes as complete packages, not only fees. With no binding cash limit, the maximum weighted product is αα(1−α)1−αS, so the mode with greater positive S wins this particular rule. This follows by substituting the gains, not by adding payments to benefits. When constraints bind, compute the attainable product for each mode. With multiple tied modes, report the tie; uniqueness of the transfer within a mode does not prove uniqueness of the whole package.

3. Academic partnership: create value, then negotiate its division

Case A — an institute and a methods laboratory

Decision and preparation record. Cedar Institute U wants a supported methods program for a specified working-learner cohort. A separately governed Methods Laboratory L can deliver it. All values and costs refer to the coming semester in kCU. U's feasible fallback is an already available internal program yielding net benefit 20; L's compatible fallback is a different job yielding net profit 10 after all its costs. The laboratory cannot do both jobs in the same staff slot. U has 70 kCU authorized and available for the upfront transfer, with no additional borrowing. Internal valuations are stipulated decision inputs, not measured learning gains or universally monetized educational worth. Both alternatives preserve the stated minimum teaching and independent-assessment standard under the case assumptions.

Complete delivery modes; no unlisted costs or payments
ModeU gross valueL delivery costJoint payoffGain over outside payoffs
S — standard schedule100406030
H — hybrid schedule90256535

The inputs(outside U,outside L,upfront ceiling) are (20,10,70). The hybrid schedule lowers U's value by 10 but saves 15 in delivery costs; net joint gain rises by 5. That does not prove real hybrid teaching is equivalent or cheaper. It is the explicit premise to verify before implementing this fictional choice. Staff, students and an assessment reviewer matter even though only two organizations receive modeled payoffs; unmet educational or access requirements cannot be silently bought away by this arithmetic.

Acceptable transfers and choice. Standard delivery requires t≥40+10=50 and t≤min(100−20,70)=70, giving [50,70]. Its symmetric unconstrained transfer is 65, within that interval: payoffs (35,25), gains (15,15). Hybrid requires t≥35 and t≤70; its symmetric transfer is 105/2, giving payoffs (75/2,55/2), gains (35/2,35/2). The intervals and symmetric decisions are ((50,70,65,35,25),(35,70,105/2,75/2,55/2)). Their gain products are (225,1225/4). H wins the stipulated symmetric rule and makes each party 5/2 better off than the symmetric S package. This is a comparison of complete packages under the same rule, not a claim that any hybrid fee dominates every standard fee.

Full negotiation record. “U initially requested standard delivery for 50; L requested 70. Both prices lie in the standard acceptance interval, but they divide gains very differently: at 50 L only matches its fallback, whereas at 70 U gains 10 and L gains 20. The facilitator separated U's interest in accessible, rigorous delivery from the requested timetable, and L's need to cover staff opportunity cost from its initial price. Both reviewed the alternative hybrid design and recorded the value reduction and cost saving rather than calling the lower fee an automatic efficiency gain. They agreed to use equal gains as this exercise's distribution convention, conditional on verifying the educational and staffing premises. The resulting proposed package is H at 52.5, not an executed commitment. Each organization retains its fallback until the required checks and authorization are complete.”

Complete proposed term sheet. “Scope: one semester of the specified cohort program using the hybrid schedule, with the agreed teaching, advising and independent assessment activities included in the 25 cost. Consideration: U pays 52.5 kCU to L before delivery; U's finance lead verifies the 70 cash ceiling and L confirms the 25 delivery budget. No future fees or learning claims fund the upfront transfer. Conditions before commitment: academic leads approve the same stated capability standard and access arrangements, the laboratory verifies staff availability, and each actual authorized decision maker approves the package. Evidence: preserve the scope version, schedule, resource quote, permitted support and assessment specification. Completion is judged from the promised delivered activities and actual learner evidence, without guaranteeing every learner succeeds.

“Change and dispute process: a changed quote, cohort scope or failed standard check stops new commitment pending a common revised payoff and resource table. The two leads first reconcile facts and record the point of disagreement; if unresolved, a jointly designated facilitator clarifies options and the actual decision owners decide whether to revise, defer or use the available alternatives. No facilitator may waive a cash limit or educational standard. Before signing any actual agreement, qualified institutional reviewers must specify the applicable responsibilities, payment protections, cancellation treatment and dispute provisions. This classroom term sheet neither establishes enforceability nor invents a universal legal remedy.”

Stakeholder memo. “We prefer H at 52.5 only under the recorded quality, access, cost and fallback premises. The smaller fee alone is not our reason: joint net value rises from 60 to 65 and the chosen sharing rule increases each party's gain. Students need the promised learning conditions; staff need an achievable workload; funders need the authorized use of cash. Report actual delivery and outcomes separately. If an academic lead cannot substantiate the minimum standard, reject or redesign H even though its monetary calculation looks attractive. An agreement between the two budget holders is not proof that every affected stakeholder has been served.”

4. A coalition can object even when each member gains individually

A coalition is a group able to implement an alternative together. A transferable-payoff model assigns each group S a net value v(S) in common units; its members may divide that value through feasible transfers. Assume the group's value does not depend on how outsiders organize, all listed alternatives are actually available, and the listed money can be transferred. These strong assumptions exclude many real political, professional and legal constraints. The empty coalition has value zero. The grand coalition includes all members.

An allocation x distributes the grand coalition's value: Σxi=v(N). It is in the core if every coalition receives at least what it can obtain separately, Σi∈Sxi≥v(S). This is the no-blocking definition in the scoped MIT notes, not an equilibrium prediction for every bargaining process. If a coalition receives less than v(S), divide the positive difference among its members to make every one strictly better off. Conversely, making every member strictly better off requires a total greater than their current sum; it is impossible if that sum is already at least v(S). This proves both directions under transferable payoffs.

Core membership need not imply equality, ethical acceptability, legal permissibility, unanimous enthusiasm or uniqueness. The core can be empty even when total joint production exceeds every disjoint alternative. An empty core means no division of the stated grand total can withstand all listed coalitional alternatives. Better facilitation might reveal mistaken values or improve the productive arrangement, but it cannot make inconsistent inequalities true.

Case B — three financial advisory firms share a service contract

Decision contract. Three fictional financial advisory firms A, B and C consider a shared model-validation service using permitted inputs. Values below are one-year net distributable monetary payoffs in kCU after all delivery and administration costs, on a common settlement date. Every coalition can fund its delivery costs; settlement transfers among its members are feasible and unrestricted in this toy model. Separate coalitions can operate without changing each other's value. These are stipulated complete-information opportunities, not actual banking permissions, forecast evidence or legal authority. Data access, client duties and approval rights would require separate actual review.

All coalition alternatives; net payoffs, not gross revenue
CoalitionValue
empty0
A4
B3
C2
AB14
AC12
BC10
ABC20

Full core and proof. Individual participation requires xA≥4, xB≥3 and xC≥2. The pair conditions are A+B≥14, A+C≥12 and B+C≥10. With total 20, these are respectively C≤6, B≤8 and A≤10. Thus the entire core is exactly the intersection of the plane A+B+C=20 with the box 4≤A≤10, 3≤B≤8, 2≤C≤6. This is a necessary-and-sufficient description: reversing each subtraction recovers every coalition inequality, and all eight coalitions are covered.

A more useful global parameterization is A=10−a, B=8−b, C=6−c with a,b,c≥0 and a+b+c=4. The original lower bounds impose no further restriction because each slack is at most 4. The core is therefore the triangle with vertices ((6,8,6),(10,4,6),(10,8,2)), including its edges and interior. Every point is a convex combination of these vertices with weights a/4,b/4,c/4 respectively. No grid search is needed to establish that description.

A defensible proposed allocation. Take x=(8,7,5). Its singleton margins are (4,4,3), pair margins AB/AC/BC are (1,1,2), and its total is 20: ((8,7,5),(4,4,3),(1,1,2),20). No listed coalition can make all its members better off. The choice of this interior point still requires a distribution rationale: the participants propose it as a negotiated split recognizing A's stronger standalone and pair alternatives while leaving every pair strictly above its own value. The model does not establish a unique fair split. An equal split of 20/3 each would fail AB: their joint 40/3 is below 14. They could split 14 as (7,7), giving each an improvement of 1/3. Individual gains over (4,3,2) therefore do not suffice.

Complete negotiation and stakeholder record. “The facilitator first confirmed that the singleton and pair opportunities use the same cost and settlement boundary as the grand contract. A proposed equal split was tested against all alternatives rather than accepted because it sounded neutral. AB's documented blocking opportunity led the group to map the whole feasible core. The delegates proposed (8,7,5), disclosed that it is one of many admissible distributions and sent it to their actual decision owners for review. The service lead must verify the shared work plan and the finance leads must reconcile the net payoff estimates and ability to transfer. Clients require delivery, confidentiality and appropriate professional review; mathematical agreement among firms does not discharge those obligations. No candidate split is authorized until these separate conditions are met.”

Complete proposed agreement record. “Scope: the specified one-year common service, with each member's work, reviewer and deliverable recorded before commitment. Economic allocation: net distributable total 20, assigned 8 to A, 7 to B and 5 to C on the common settlement date after the listed costs; reconcile the actual revenue/cost account before any distribution. The example assumes the total is known. A real agreement must explicitly allocate shortfalls, overruns and control rights rather than treat these proposed amounts as guaranteed. No participant may promise the same staff or revenue to overlapping coalitions simultaneously. Each firm confirms its delivery funding and authorized consent.

“Review and escalation: preserve the eight-value table, cost basis and evidence for each outside opportunity. If a value or delivery obligation changes, recompute all constraints before relying on the old split. Disputed facts go first to a common reconciliation with each firm's finance lead; unresolved allocation disagreements go to the authorized owners with the feasible set and alternatives attached. Mediation may help clarify interests but cannot create an unmodeled cash source. Draft actual exit, data-use, change-control and dispute provisions through the appropriate institutional process. No signature, enforceable right or completed service is claimed by this exercise.”

An empty-core conflict and a real repair. Now suppose verified changes make each pair worth 15, while singleton values remain (4,3,2) and the grand total stays 20. Each pair requires a sum at least 15; adding the three conditions yields 2(A+B+C)≥45. But feasibility gives 2×20=40. No split works. Yet every disjoint alternative produces at most 19: AB+C gives 17, AC+B gives 18, BC+A gives 19 and all singletons give 9. The grand total is larger than each, but the overlapping pair demands cannot all be satisfied.

If an actual productivity improvement or separately justified outside contribution raises only the grand total to G, the pair sum proof requires G≥45/2. At G=45/2, allocation (15/2,15/2,15/2) satisfies all singletons and all pairs, proving sufficiency and a minimum increase of 5/2 from 20. The repair tuple(total,additional value,allocation) is (45/2,5/2,(15/2,15/2,15/2)). The allocation is unique at that threshold because three pair inequalities sum to equality, so each pair sum must equal 15. Relabeling the existing 20 or borrowing with an equal repayment obligation does not create the required net value. A donor's cost and authorization must be included in any broader welfare or governance claim; the model's three-member core alone omits that stakeholder.

Full conflict-resolution memo. “Under the revised pair values, withdraw the claim that a fairer division of 20 will settle all parties. Preserve the old and revised evidence and show the contradiction 40<45. Ask the service designers whether a documented change can create at least 2.5 additional net value for the grand service without changing the pair alternatives. If it can, recompute and review the proposed threshold split (7.5,7.5,7.5). If it cannot, return an unresolved coalition-stability problem to the decision owners and examine a different project, partition or explicitly different agreement concept. Do not promise that an empty core predicts which coalition will form, or that a vote removes an available exit opportunity. The chosen process still needs actual authorization and stakeholder protection.”

5. Resolve the kind of disagreement actually present

Distinguish a factual dispute, an interest conflict, a distribution conflict and an authority problem. A disputed cost calls for a common scope and evidence check. A timetable conflict may admit another design. A disagreement over sharing an agreed surplus requires a disclosed distribution choice. A negotiator lacking approval needs the actual decision owner. Treating every problem as poor communication can hide an infeasible mandate; treating every disagreement as bad faith can prevent an otherwise workable redesign.

Use a versioned record of proposals, assumptions, objections and decisions. Ask each party to restate the other's concern accurately before answering it. Separate a conditional offer from an accepted commitment, and an accepted commitment from completed performance. Contingent terms can attach different actions to a clearly observable future condition, but the condition, evidence, verifier, timing and feasible responses must be specified. A clause tied to “satisfactory cooperation” may merely move the conflict into an undefined measurement. No term can eliminate every contingency; identify who must decide when the specified model no longer applies.

Exercises

  1. For standard delivery in Case A, derive the funded acceptable transfer interval. Solve the weighted-gain rule for U weights 2/3 and 1/4. Give both payoffs and gains, and explain why the cash ceiling changes one solution. Write a concise complete negotiating recommendation that distinguishes the rule from fairness.
  2. Raise only L's net outside payoff to 25. Recompute both modes' intervals and symmetric funded decisions; compare gain products and choose. Then raise L's outside payoff to 46 instead. Explain why there is no agreement and why subtracting the outside payoff twice is wrong.
  3. Restore original outside payoffs but reduce U's upfront payment ceiling to 40. Compare both modes and give the symmetric-rule feasible choice, payoffs and gains. Explain why positive joint surplus does not make standard delivery fundable.
  4. Before any irreversible commitment, the registrar verifies either 24 confirmed eligible roster members (H gross value 90) or 16 (value 70); other counts are outside this two-state model; delivery cost remains 25 and both original outside options remain available at that date. Derive the symmetric acceptable transfer in each state. Test the original unconditional 52.5 fee in the low state and write a complete conditional term that specifies observation, verification, timing and a stop rule. No probabilities are supplied.
  5. Prove the whole original consortium core, not just one feasible point. Test the equal split and proposed (8,7,5), give an actual blocking allocation when one fails, and write a complete stakeholder explanation of what core membership does and does not establish.
  6. Set all three pair values to 15 and keep singletons (4,3,2). Prove that grand totals 20 and 22 cannot have a core allocation. Find the smallest grand total that can, its allocation and uniqueness at that boundary. Explain why redistributing the original total is not a repair.
  7. Starting from the original consortium, change only AB's value from 14 to 17. Derive the new full core and its vertices. Does (8,7,5) survive? Give a blocking proposal if not, and explain whose residual upper bound changes.
  8. Write a complete review memo after two verified changes: H's delivery cost rises to 45, with all other Case A data unchanged; in Case B all pair values are 15 and the grand total is still 20. A negotiator proposes keeping the old hybrid fee and adopting (8,7,5) by a two-to-one vote. Recompute the relevant comparisons, explain what remains unapproved or infeasible, name responsible reviewers and propose the next action without inventing authority or new resources.
Complete solutions and evaluation criteria

1. Power convention and payment capacity are separate

The funded interval is [50,70], with S=30. At α=2/3, t*=50+(1/3)30=60: payoffs (40,20), gains (20,10). At α=1/4, unconstrained t*=50+(3/4)30=145/2, above the ceiling 70. The product increases with t up to 72.5, so the unique funded choice is 70: payoffs (30,30), gains (10,20). Result(transfer,payoff U,payoff L,gain U,gain L) is ((60,40,20,20,10),(70,30,30,10,20)). Recommendation: “Use the declared weight only after the parties agree on its purpose and verify the alternatives. Under U weight 2/3 propose 60; under weight 1/4 the funded ceiling truncates the preferred transfer to 70. Neither convention proves the split fair, and neither authorizes spending 72.5 from 70 cash.” Credit the interval, unconstrained versus funded distinction, correct gains and actual recommendation.

2. A stronger fallback reduces the available gains

With dL 25, S delivery has gains 15, interval[65,70] and unconstrained symmetric transfer 72.5; the funded transfer 70 gives payoffs(30,30), gains(10,5), product 50. H has gains 20, interval[50,70] and transfer 60, payoffs(30,35), gains(10,10), product 100. Choose H under the stated rule. The tuples(lower,upper,transfer,payoff U,payoff L,product) are ((65,70,70,30,30,50),(50,70,60,30,35,100)). With dL 46, standard's lower endpoint 86 exceeds upper 70, and hybrid's lower endpoint 71 exceeds upper 70; joint gains are−6 and−1 respectively. Both also have negative joint gains, so removing the cash ceiling alone would not restore participation. L's agreement payoff is t−c; compare it once with 46. Equivalently, require gain t−c−46≥0, not ≥46. Credit consistent net accounts and the two infeasibility demonstrations.

3. A valuable agreement can still be unfunded

Standard needs t≥50 but permits t≤40, so its interval is empty although S=30. H has interval[35,40]; its unconstrained symmetric transfer 52.5 is unavailable. On this interval the product increases toward 52.5, so choose 40. U receives 50 and L 15; their gains are 30 and 5, product 150. The result is (35,40,40,50,15,30,5,150). The institution's valuation 90 does not give it 90 cash. A new funding arrangement would be a changed problem requiring its own dated resources and costs. Credit interval feasibility and conditional optimization, not merely the positive surplus.

4. Conditional terms need a verifiable condition

At V 90, S 35 and t 52.5, payoffs 37.5/27.5. At V 70, S 15, interval[35,50] and symmetric t 42.5, payoffs 27.5/17.5, gains 7.5 each. The low-state tuple(upper,transfer,payoffs,gains) is (50,85/2,(55/2,35/2),(15/2,15/2)). Keeping fee 52.5 in that state would give U 17.5, below its fallback 20, though L receives 27.5.

Term: “Before payment or irreversible preparation, the jointly appointed registrar verifies the dated count of confirmed eligible roster members: exactly 24 selects the high state and exactly 16 the low state; any other count is outside this two-state agreement. Both parties receive the record and may correct factual errors. A verified high state uses H at 52.5; a verified low state uses H at 42.5, with the same included cost 25 and agreed delivery standard. No new commitment occurs while the state is disputed or if costs, available cash, scope or either fallback has changed; the actual authorized owners then compare updated terms or use available alternatives. Before signing, the parties must agree how eligibility, confirmation and authorized access to the dated register are verified; no count is treated as an achieved learning outcome.” No expected fee or expected welfare is identified without probabilities. Credit both states, the failing unconditional offer and a complete implementable-in-principle clause with its remaining real specification disclosed.

5. Global stability under the modeled alternatives

The pair inequalities and total 20 give A≤10,B≤8,C≤6; singleton lower bounds are 4,3,2. Write x=(10,8,6)−(a,b,c), with nonnegative slacks summing 4. Each slack cannot exceed 4, so all singleton bounds hold; conversely every core allocation has precisely such slacks. This proves the triangle and its three displayed vertices completely. Equal 20/3 fails AB because 40/3<14; allocation(7,7) within AB's value 14 improves each by 1/3. At(8,7,5), singleton margins 4/4/3 and pair margins 1/1/2 are nonnegative and total 20 exhausts the value.

Memo: “The proposed split survives every stated single-firm and pair opportunity; equal division does not. This is a stability test under transferable payoffs, known values and available coalition alternatives. It neither proves ethical fairness nor validates the service estimate, client protections or decision authority. Record why this particular point was selected from the full triangle, preserve each firm's consent and require actual scope/funding review before commitment.” Credit both directions of the core characterization, an actual strict block and all limitations.

6. A minimum repair needs additional net value

Adding the three pair inequalities gives 2 G≥45. G 20 and G 22 imply 40 and 44 respectively, so both fail. At G 45/2, x=(15/2,15/2,15/2) gives each pair 15 and each singleton more than its fallback. Necessity and this witness prove the threshold, and the minimum increase from 20 is 5/2. Equality of the sum forces every pair condition to bind; subtracting any two pair equations and using their sum gives the unique equal allocation. A different distribution of 20 cannot change 2 G=40. A borrowing receipt with matching repayment is not net surplus; any external subsidy needs a real source and review of the omitted contributor. Credit global impossibility, sufficiency, uniqueness and the resource interpretation.

7. A pair's improved option limits the third member

AB≥17 becomes C≤3; A≤10 and B≤8 remain. With sum 20 and nonnegative slacks from(10,8,3), total slack is 1. Singleton minima do not bind further. The complete new triangle has vertices ((9,8,3),(10,7,3),(10,8,2)). The old split gives AB 15<17. AB can instead take(9,8), improving each by 1 while using their 17. C's residual upper bound falls from 6 to 3 because the complement AB became stronger; no claim that C became less productive follows. A stronger coalition opportunity changes feasible distribution, not automatically the grand total or moral merit. Credit the global slack argument and actual block.

8. An evidence-based rejection of an attractive old agreement

“The verified hybrid cost 45 changes its joint payoff to 45 and gains to 15. Its interval is[55,70], symmetric fee 62.5, payoffs 27.5/17.5 and product 225/4. The old 52.5 fee gives the laboratory 7.5, below its outside profit 10. Standard remains feasible at 65, payoffs 35/25 and product 225; it beats the revised hybrid under the original symmetric rule and gives each party 7.5 more. Propose standard at 65 only after the academic lead reconfirms scope/standard and finance checks cost, cash and fallback availability; do not sign the old hybrid sheet.” The revised hybrid tuple(lower,upper,transfer,payoffs,product) is (55,70,125/2,(55/2,35/2),225/4).

“For the consortium, verified pair values 15 with total 20 imply an empty core. The proposed(8,7,5) has pair sums 15,13,12; AC can use(9,6) to make both better off within 15. A two-to-one vote does not remove an alternative that our model says remains available, and no supplied rule establishes authority to bind the dissenter. The three finance leads must retain the revised opportunity evidence and the service designers must test whether at least 2.5 additional net value can be created. Send the contradiction and conditional threshold repair to the actual decision owners. Until a supported redesign or different authorized arrangement exists, record the agreement as unresolved. Do not fabricate a subsidy, misconduct, legal exit rule or completed consent.” Credit both revised comparisons, the actual coalition block, named responsibilities and truthful pending status.

Teach-back and delayed retention

Teach-back. Explain why a fallback differs from a demand, why transfers cancel from joint value, and why individual participation is weaker than coalitional stability. Guide: L's fallback 10 is net profit from another available job; standard fee 50 just matches it. Moving the fee does not change V−c. Equal 20/3 exceeds every original singleton value yet AB can improve both members by dividing 14. The math checks specified alternatives; actual permission and stakeholder obligations remain separate.

Delayed task. Restore original academic inputs but give H cost 30. Find its symmetric fee and compare it with standard. Then use consortium pair values 15 and grand total 23, keeping singletons unchanged; describe the whole core. Answer: H now has gains 30 and fee 55, payoffs 35/25, product 225, tying standard's symmetric package in payoffs/product. Report the mode tie; a declared secondary criterion or evidence is needed. For the consortium each x≤8 and total 23, so write x=(8,8,8)−nonnegative slacks summing 1. This yields vertices(7,8,8),(8,7,8),(8,8,7), with singleton bounds slack. The tuple is (55,(35,25),225,((7,8,8),(8,7,8),(8,8,7))). A printed answer is not evidence of unaided negotiation judgment.

Sources and continuation

The official PON introductory body supports the narrow BATNA comparison concept; linked reports, tagged articles and empirical advice were not imported. Manea's MIT notes, inspected at physical pages 1–3 for transferable payoffs/core definitions and page 11 for the Nash objective and its scope, provide method context. The document itself is dated January 19,2017 despite the Spring 2016 host path. Its general balancedness theorem, implementation models and later axiomatic proof are outside the claims made here. All cases, proofs, terms and exercises are original. Governance, fiduciary duties and integrity next examines decision rights and jurisdiction-aware responsibilities that a numerical agreement alone cannot establish.

Sources and further study

  • What is your Best Alternative to a Negotiated Agreement? — Narrow BATNA benchmark definition; chapter independently specifies feasible dated alternatives, consistent net accounts and original cases.
  • Cooperative Games — Definition-level transferable-payoff/core and symmetric Nash objective context. Original two-mode constrained weighted-gains proof and complete three-member core/repair proof supplied in manuscript.
